identity.title: Unilaterally absent or markedly reduced breath sounds (+/- tracheal deviation as late tension sign)

technique.how: Auscultate both hemithoraces at matched anterior, lateral and posterior points during quiet then deep breathing, comparing each site directly with its mirror-image contralateral site. Note whether breath sounds are absent, markedly reduced or merely asymmetric, and check tracheal position in the suprasternal notch.
technique.prerequisites: Quiet room, skin contact (not through clothing), patient able to breathe on request; in trauma, examine during primary survey with the patient supine.
technique.contraindications: None; do not delay decompression of a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax to complete the exam.

interpretation.positive_finding: Breath sounds clearly absent or much reduced on one side compared with the other, with or without hyperresonance (pneumothorax) or dullness (effusion/consolidation).
interpretation.negative_finding: Symmetric, normal-intensity vesicular breath sounds bilaterally; this lowers but does not exclude small pneumothorax, effusion or pneumonia.
interpretation.pitfalls: Sounds transmit across the mediastinum and the finding is insensitive (pooled sensitivity around 0.5-0.7), so a normal exam cannot rule out pneumothorax. Obesity, COPD hyperinflation, shallow breathing and noisy resuscitation bays reduce reliability.
interpretation.changes_what: Unilateral absence after chest trauma or with hypotension: treat as pneumothorax/hemothorax until imaged (POCUS/CXR); with dullness, evaluate for effusion or consolidation.

estimates.population: Adults with blunt or penetrating chest trauma (5 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)
estimates.location: Table 3, row 'Abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds - (Hemato) pneumothorax'

estimates.population: Adults with acute respiratory symptoms or suspected pneumonia (6 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)
estimates.location: Table 3, row 'Abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds - Pneumonia'

sources.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Straus SE. Does this patient have a pleural effusion? JAMA. 2009;301(3):309-317.
Kalantri S, Joshi R, Lokhande T, et al. Accuracy and reliability of physical signs in the diagnosis of pleural effusion. Respir Med. 2007;101(3):431-438.
Metlay JP, Kapoor WN, Fine MJ. Does this patient have community-acquired pneumonia? Diagnosing pneumonia by history and physical examination. JAMA. 1997;278(17):1440-1445.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on auscultation alone to exclude pneumothorax in an unstable trauma patient or before positive-pressure ventilation; use POCUS or CXR.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hypotension, distended neck veins or tracheal deviation is tension physiology: decompress immediately, do not wait for imaging.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Kalantri 2007 reported excellent inter-observer agreement for breath sounds (kappa 0.84-0.89) among two blinded physicians (Abstract).

extraction_notes: Trauma estimate is Arts 2020 Table 3 pooled row for 'abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds' vs CXR in chest-trauma cohorts (Sci Rep, PMC7192898); note reference standard is CXR, not CT, so occult pneumothoraces count as negatives and sensitivity is overestimated. Pneumonia row from the same table (mixed primary care/ED/inpatient). Pleural effusion: the JAMA RCE (Wong 2009, PMID 19155458) abstract reports only percussion and fremitus LRs and full text is not open access; Kalantri 2007 abstract gives only LR ranges (1.48-8.14 positive; 0.13-0.71 negative) without a breath-sound-specific number, so no pleural-effusion estimate is entered. Tracheal deviation has no diagnostic-accuracy data located; it is described as a late tension sign on consensus grounds only.
